# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: My pick, could read captions while watching faces, appears word for word in the belief and in the test box, and nothing is reworded.
screens.why7: The picked row is a sound ability on the single could-they measure, with the right ability bar and room to go either way, but the step the mechanism depends on most (a phone that is with them and online) is no longer on the list, which bends the rule that it is never missing.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? Could read captions while watching faces (picked) / Had their phone with them and online.

screens.why1: After the screens on how the glasses fit into their day, asking what they do better than today's way is the obvious next step before the study turns to adoption and price.
screens.why2: The question is plain, and 'one benefit a line, up to four, each up to 9 words' tells me exactly what to type; the example 'less time on it each week' isn't how my people talk about conversations, but it reads as a generic example rather than a word I have to decode.
screens.why3: I know exactly what our wearers gain over phone captions, hearing aids and lipreading, so I can answer this from my own customers' words.
screens.why4: There is a free-text box for up to four benefits, and the single 'I'm not sure' chip is the right escape, since it leaves the dimension out rather than inventing a gain.
screens.why5: My row 'More of the talk followed without asking for repeats' sits on the screen as I typed it, and Keel has added nothing of its own here except the frame.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 benefits of at most 9 words each, framed against today's way ('what ... today's way does not give them'), with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, so the card's shape is met and my nine-word noun-phrase row fits it.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what it does better than today's way, Keel reads my benefit back for me to check before it becomes the belief, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I can read it at once, but 'more of the talk followed' is a clumsy passive I would never say, and it makes the belief read oddly as 'would have given them more of the talk followed'.
screens.why3: Following a table conversation without making my wife or friends repeat themselves is exactly the gain my customers describe, and I know it first-hand.
screens.why4: One row holding my one lead benefit, no overlap, no number I did not write, and room to add up to four.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed, following more without asking for repeats, and the strangers never see it.
screens.why7: My lead benefit is the single row, the belief carries it whole against the moment it went wrong (the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people), not any last occasion, and the bar is the card's one in three saying no difference or worse.
screens.instead: Row: Following more of the talk without asking for repeats -- belief: ...would have let them follow more of the talk without asking for repeats.

screens.why1: Right after I typed my advantage and Keel checked it, this screen shows me what it kept and what it will test, which is the obvious next step before moving on.
screens.why2: The row is clear to me, but 'would have given them more of the talk followed without asking for repeats' is clunky; I had to read the belief twice to parse 'the talk followed'.
screens.why3: Losing the thread at a table and having to ask people to repeat is exactly what our wearers live with every week, and I know it from my own friend's story and our users.
screens.why4: One row, one gain, nine words, no overlap and no number I didn't write, which is a complete list for the single benefit I lead with.
screens.why5: 'Following more without asking anyone to repeat' became 'More of the talk followed without asking for repeats', which is the same gain in nearly my words, and nothing was put aside.
screens.why7: My leading benefit is kept as the one row within 9 words, the belief carries it against the hard-case moment (the last time they lost the conversation, not any last conversation), and the four-rung bar of no more than 1 in 3 'no difference'/'worse' lets it both hold and fail.
screens.instead: Row: 'Following more of the talk without asking for repeats'; belief: 'For most, with it, the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, they would have followed more of it without asking for repeats.'

screens.why1: After fit and advantage, asking what effort it takes to start is the obvious next question about my glasses, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me, and the 9-word limit made it easy to type 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations; Charge the glasses every day'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a wearer has to do day to day: put the glasses on for the conversation and keep them charged.
screens.why4: The box took my two efforts as separate rows, and 'I'm not sure' fits as the way out for a founder who can't name the effort.
screens.why5: My two efforts sit on the screen as I typed them, nothing reworded.
screens.why7: Both rows are single base-form efforts of at most 9 words that the wearer takes themselves, both are new habits of use, neither repeats Compatibility (phone online, captions while watching faces) or Purchase friction, and a stranger could answer either way, so the belief can hold or fail; 'I'm not sure' is the founder's escape the card allows.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it takes to start, checking Keel's draft of those efforts is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Wearing the glasses in conversations and charging them daily are exactly how I'd say it to my own customers.
screens.why3: Both are things a deaf or hard-of-hearing wearer does themselves every day and knows whether they'd do.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in plain words, but the intro repeats the title and pairing the glasses to the phone, the real one-time setup, is missing and not offered as a suggestion.
screens.why5: Wearing the caption glasses is my own effort as I typed it, and the daily charge is a true cost of the hardware I sell.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form efforts the wearer takes themselves, in the third person, under 9 words, two of the allowed 1 to 4, with no sign-off and nothing overlapping Compatibility or Purchase friction, so a Yes or a No answers the belief either way.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Wear the caption glasses in conversations · Charge the glasses every day · Pair the glasses with their phone once (suggested: the one-time setup before first use).

screens.why1: This screen comes right after I listed and checked what my wearers have to do to start, so it is obvious why it asks me to pick the one effort most likely to stop them.
screens.why2: Both rows are plain words my wearers and I use every day, and the title asks one clear thing, though the intro's 'nothing is reworded here' is Keel's housekeeping rather than my words.
screens.why3: I know my wearers, and putting visible caption glasses on in front of hearing people at the table is the step they hesitate over, so I can answer this from what I hear every week.
screens.why4: The two efforts are distinct and in plain words: wearing them in the conversation itself, and a daily charging habit. Between them they cover the new habit of use, and nothing is missing that would stop my wearers more.
screens.why5: My row is shown exactly as I saved it, and Keel's charging suggestion sits last without displacing it, so the screen still means what I typed.
screens.why7: Both are the wearer's own effort on the one measure (would they take it on), my row comes first with one Keel suggestion last, nothing repeats Compatibility or Purchase friction, and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' can be supported or refuted by Yes / Only if / Probably not / No, with I can't tell on the item.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, asking whether to collect emails from people who'd try it is the obvious last step, and as AirCaps with 15-day free returns I want exactly that list.
screens.why2: Short and plain: 'Offer a pilot?' with the hint showing the exact line people will see leaves nothing to reread.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers to leave an email is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks and my pick is kept, but 'try this for real' sits a little loose against a $599 pair of glasses ordered with free returns, a purchase rather than a free pilot.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? -- People who say yes see: "Would you try the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Saving my answers right before the study goes out to strangers is the obvious last step of the flow.
screens.why2: "Lock and record the face Keel preselects" made me stop: I had to guess that "face" means the AI interviewer's avatar, not my respondents' faces, a worry I'd have since my glasses sit in front of people's faces.
screens.why3: Whether to keep Keel's pick and save is my own decision about my own study, fully answerable.
screens.why4: The pick bundles locking, recording and accepting Keel's preselected face into one choice, and nothing visible lets me save but change the face.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea's wording is restated or changed here; it only saves what I already set.
screens.instead: Save your answers -- options: "Save and keep the interviewer Keel picked" / "Save and choose a different interviewer"

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will take the study is the obvious last step after saving my answers, right before the link goes out.
screens.why2: The heading 'New link' does not say it is asking how my respondents will answer; I only understand that from the option descriptions.
screens.why3: I know my people are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can easily judge which format will work for them.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and complete, but for a deaf audience the 'AI interviewer' option, where a face 'asks each question aloud' and they answer 'by talking', reads oddly unless it says the video is captioned.
screens.why5: Nothing about my product or roles is changed or leaked here; it is only the delivery format.
screens.instead: How will the people you send this to answer it? Read and tap (they read each question and tap or type) / AI interviewer (a face on video asks each question aloud, with captions; they answer by talking, typing or tapping) / Let them choose

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title with "3 beliefs: 3 holding" beside it, each card carries its own 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and the page says the verdict is the worst card, so I know both the answer and the numbers behind it.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over 7 people, and where my bar sits (5 of 7), all on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and beliefs are recognisably mine, but the statement under the title is garbled ("the wearer the app on the lightweight glasses shows... and gets back live captions inside the lens"), and the relative-advantage line is clumsy: it is not how I would describe AirCaps.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do with a clean pass: whether to move to the commercial stage, or to look at the 3 people who would only wear the glasses on a condition.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but a unanimous 7 of 7 is shown with no word that seven is a small group, which reads firmer than it is.
screens.instead: Holding up on all three, but only 7 people answered, so read it as a strong early signal rather than proof. 3 would wear the glasses only on a condition: open Adoption friction to see which conditions, then check the price on the commercial page. And describe my solution properly: AirCaps glasses show live captions of nearby speech inside the lens, so the wearer follows the conversation while still watching faces.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to the one question, over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar at 5 of 7 with all 7 cells for me, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Could read captions while watching faces" is the condition I picked on Compatibility, and the belief reads it after "Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults" in my own words.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me this fit is not the blocker and points me at Adoption friction, which is a concrete place to look next.
screens.why_b5: The count line does say "a small group: a lean, not a call", but the So line then states flatly that this is "not what will stop them" of all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, from 7 people, 3 of whom said only "most of the time".
screens.instead: Say it as a lean: "Among these 7, reading captions while watching faces did not look like the blocker (3 only most of the time); Adoption friction, below, did."

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said better against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip with its marker at 5 of 7 reads cleanly, but the chart's 'Better · 7 7 a lot · 0 a little' runs the total and the a-lot count together and takes a second look to parse.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Relative advantage and carries my benefit, 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats', inside the belief about the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, as I checked it.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates that all 7 imagined it better and points me to Adoption friction, but it does not say what a unanimous 'a lot better' means for the idea, such as leading the pitch with this gain while the wearing question stays open.
screens.why_b5: The small n, the 'lean, not a call' and the hypothetical framing are all stated, but the question described AirCaps as 'an app', when it is caption glasses, so the 7 of 7 'a lot better' was answered about something other than what I sell.
screens.instead: Ask about 'AirCaps, caption glasses paired to your phone', not 'an app', and have the So line say: 'All 7 of 7 said a lot better: a strong lean on the gain itself; whether they would actually wear the glasses is the open question, in Adoption friction below.'

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits beside 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the belief held and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts plain yes against the comfort condition against probably not and no over the 7 who answered, and the strip puts my bar at 5 of 7, all readable at first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the effort I picked, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line points to what would win over the 3 conditional yeses, but it never names the thing to act on: comfort over long wear and a chance to try before buying (my 15-day returns).
screens.why_b5: n is visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said, but the So line promises the three's reasons are below when their quotes are about stage lights, audience mics and seat choice, not comfort, and the same condition stands for all three as if each had said it.
screens.instead: Holding up, 7 of 7 would wear them, a small group's lean; 3 only if the glasses stay comfortable through long talks, so lead with all-day comfort and the 15-day free returns as the way to find out.

screens.why_b1: The box says Adoption friction held, 7 of 7, and puts the bar of 5 of 7 and the 3 on a condition right under it, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the dimension and the wording I checked, as revision 24 set it.
screens.why_b4: The screen only says 'what they added' and never says what the conditions mean for me, for example offering a trial loan before the order or fixing audience pickup in large halls.
screens.why_b5: Each of the three quotes is tagged 'Only if they stay comfortable through long talks', followed by a dangling 'for', but none of them mentions comfort (one is a seating workaround, one asks for a trial under stage lights, one is about mic range), so the condition looks like something they did not say.
screens.why_b6: A borrow-before-you-buy trial under theatre lighting, the four mics missing audience questions in a big hall, and a single-sided-deaf user who manages with seat choice are all things I did not type and can act on.
screens.instead: Held, 7 of 7 (3 on a condition, all on comfort through long talks). What they added points elsewhere: let people try a pair at a real event before ordering, and make sure the mics pick up audience questions in big rooms, not just the speaker.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check that I actually talk with hearing people regularly before asking me anything else.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how deaf people talk about everyone else, so I'd answer this straight away, though I might wonder for a second whether chatting through an interpreter or by passing notes counts as talking.
screens.why3: I know whether I've been in conversations with hearing people this week, at work, at the shops or with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No covers it, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of anybody's product shows here, and "hearing people" is our own word, not an outsider's.
screens.why6: The question is short and clear when spoken, but "I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No." is clumsy for a yes-or-no and the guidelines say the screener should just end with "Yes or no."
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with any hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it is obvious to ask whether I actually lost the thread with them this week.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of a conversation' is exactly how I'd put it; it is one plain act in one window.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I lost the thread at the shop counter or the family dinner this week, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and a week when everyone faced me and spoke clearly is a real No; the chips belong to the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: It asks about the conversation going wrong, not about any product or the founder's terms; nothing leaks.
screens.why6: Short, one question, under 20 words, and 'Yes or no' is easy to hold when heard or captioned.
screens.why7: The gate asks the hurt (losing track), not the routine (talking with hearing people), so a Yes and a No are both true of someone and the share can support or refute the band.

screens.why1: I just said I lost track of a conversation with hearing people this week, so being shown captioning glasses next makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Live captions are something I use every day on my phone and TV, and reading words while keeping eye contact is exactly how I'd put it, since I watch faces and lips to follow along.
screens.why3: Following hearing people face to face while glancing down at a captioning app on my phone is my real life, so I can picture this against what I do now.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The product is named on purpose in an Imagine card, and nothing else leaks; it's in words I would use myself.
screens.why6: Three short plain sentences with no symbols or abbreviations, easy to take in once, though I'd be reading the captions rather than hearing them.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, glasses that show live captions of what people nearby are saying, inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while still watching the person's face.

screens.why1: Right after the card about captions on glasses, it makes sense to ask whether I could read captions and still watch people's faces, since that is what I'd actually have to do.
screens.why2: "Read captions while watching faces" is exactly how I'd say it; I lipread and use captions, so every word is mine.
screens.why3: I've never had captions in front of my eyes, only on my phone, so I'd be guessing from what juggling phone and faces is like, and "your last conversation" doesn't say it means the one with hearing people rather than with my deaf friends.
screens.why4: Easily, most of the time, sometimes, no covers it cleanly, and "I can't tell" is the honest answer for someone who's never tried it.
screens.why5: Only the idea card itself is named and nothing else of the company's plan or their words for people like me comes through.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after hearing them once, with the escape said last.
screens.why7: This is an ability with the four ability answers in order and "I can't tell" apart; it tests the step the glasses depend on most, which some of us could manage and others couldn't, so the belief can go either way.
screens.instead: Think of your last face-to-face conversation with hearing people. If captions had shown in front of your eyes, could you have read them while watching faces? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions question, it makes sense to ask whether the glasses would have helped the last time I lost track of a conversation with hearing people.
screens.why2: It's mostly plain, but 'lost the conversation' isn't how I'd say it; I'd say I 'lost track of' it, as screen 2 put it, and I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly when I last lost track at a noisy table or in a fast group chat, and I can judge whether captions on glasses would have helped me keep up and get a word in.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover what I'd honestly say, and 'I can't tell' fits if I've never tried caption glasses.
screens.why5: The card named it on purpose, and the question doesn't sell me any promised benefit; 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' is a bit formal but means what I do.
screens.why6: The four options and the escape say well as a list, but the second sentence is long by ear, and 'AirCaps, an app,' is a small aside to hold before I hear what it's asking.
screens.why7: The four options sit on one better-or-not scale with no difference and worse to refute the belief, 'I can't tell' is set apart, and the anchor is the moment it went wrong, not an ordinary chat.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you lost track of a conversation with hearing people. Would AirCaps have helped you follow and join in better, or not? A lot better / A little better / No difference / Worse; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking whether it would have helped me, asking whether I'd actually wear the glasses in conversations is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses that show captions is plain to me; I've used captions on my phone and at the theatre, so I'd answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know how I am in conversations and how I feel about wearing something on my face, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct, comfort over a long talk is a real catch for me, and I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: 'Your caption glasses' sounds like the company's product name and assumes I already own a pair, when the card only described glasses that show captions.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and the four options are easy to hold when heard once; the comfort option is the longest but still says well.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses is a step I would take myself, a new habit of use; the options sit in the fixed order with my own condition in 'Only if'; two answers count for and two against; and I can't tell sits apart.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the caption glasses whenever you talk with hearing people. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if they stay comfortable through long talks · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: After being asked whether AirCaps would have helped and whether I'd wear the glasses, it makes sense to ask what would tip it into being worth having for me.
screens.why2: Short, everyday words, and it names AirCaps instead of a bare 'it', so I can answer straight off.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I'd need, like keeping up when several people talk at once in a noisy place without looking down, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It only uses the product name already shown on the idea card and adds no new terms for me or my hearing.
screens.why6: One short question that is easy to hear once and answer aloud, with no list to hold.

typo_leaks.text: How far back should deaf or hard-of-hearing aduts look for the last time a conversation with hearingg people is too fast or too noisy to follow?
